usage: Polite request for quiet in a library, cafe, or meeting; 해 주세요 softens it
Lower your voice so others aren't disturbed; contrast 작게 말하다 (low volume)
조용히 지내요 = I'm keeping a calm, low-key life these days
Casual and slightly sharp; 좀 here adds mild irritation, not politeness
examples: 조용히 좀 해.
Be quiet, please.
Blunt 반말 between close friends or to a noisy kid; 좀 nudges it toward a plea
아기가 자니까 조용히 들어오세요.
The baby's sleeping, so come in quietly.
조용히 attaches to the action verb 들어오다 — it modifies HOW you enter
요즘은 그냥 집에서 조용히 쉬고 있어요.
These days I'm just resting quietly at home.
Here 조용히 = low-key / peacefully, not literal silence
nuance: 조용히 is the adverb of the adjective 조용하다 and stretches from literal silence ('be quiet') to a calm, low-key MANNER of doing things ('live quietly, rest peacefully'), so it's far more useful in speech than the adjective alone. The dividing line with its neighbors matters: 작게 means low in VOLUME, 가만히 means without MOVING, and 몰래 means in SECRET — only 조용히 covers undisturbing quietness. It collocates with 하다, 말하다, 지내다, 들어오다. The big English-speaker trap is treating it as the adjective: you cannot say '조용히 사람' for 'a quiet person' — that needs the adjective form 조용한 사람, while 조용히 only modifies a verb. Also mind the spelling: it ends in 히, not 이.

Using 조용히 to mean 'secretly / on the sly' — that idea is 몰래 (몰래 나가다 = sneak out). 조용히 only means without noise or fuss.

usage: The single most common pairing — hands, dishes, vegetables, fruit
Stresses cleaning all the way, leaving nothing dirty
For wiping a surface until no dirt or smudge remains
깨끗이 비웠어요 = I cleaned my plate / left nothing
examples: 손을 깨끗이 씻으세요.
Wash your hands well.
Bare everyday hygiene reminder; 깨끗이 tells you to wash THOROUGHLY, not just briefly
이사 가기 전에 집을 깨끗이 치웠어요.
I cleaned the place up thoroughly before moving out.
The move-out / deposit context where 깨끗이 = leave it spotless
지난 일은 깨끗이 잊어버렸어요.
I've cleanly put the past behind me.
Figurative: 깨끗이 잊다 = forget completely, with no residue of feeling
nuance: 깨끗이 is the adverb of 깨끗하다 and crucially means doing something so the RESULT is clean and complete, not merely 'in a clean manner' — the focus is thoroughness. It's the natural partner of 씻다, 닦다, 청소하다, 치우다, and it extends figuratively to 깨끗이 잊다 (forget cleanly) or 깨끗이 인정하다 (admit it cleanly, with no excuses). Compare 깔끔하게, which describes a tidy, neat appearance/finish (깔끔하게 정리하다), whereas 깨끗이 emphasizes the absence of dirt or residue. The notorious trap is spelling: despite all its 히-ending siblings here, this word ends in 이 — 깨끗이, never 깨끗히. Roughly, when the stem ends in a ㅅ-type sound the adverb often takes 이.

Limiting it to physical surfaces — it also means finishing/resolving something completely, as in 깨끗이 잊다 or 깨끗이 포기하다 (give up cleanly).
Reaching for 깨끗이 when you mean a neat, stylish finish; that nuance is 깔끔하게 (깔끔하게 차려입다 = dress neatly), not 깨끗이.

usage: Telling someone not to move or fidget; also 'stay out of it'
Asking someone to stop touching or meddling; 좀 adds exasperation
now that I think it over quietly
Threat form; the same 가만히 turns menacing here
examples: 가만히 있어.
Stay still.
Bare command — to a wriggling child or someone about to make things worse
가만히 좀 있어 봐, 내가 해 줄게.
Hold still a sec, I'll do it for you.
Gentle 반말; 가만히 + 있다 = don't move, vs 가만히 + 두다 = don't touch
가만히 생각해 보니 내가 실수했더라고요.
Thinking it over quietly, I realized I'd messed up.
-더라고요 reports a realization you came to; 가만히 = calmly, taking a moment
nuance: 가만히 carries two everyday senses that English splits apart: physically staying STILL (가만히 있어 = don't move) and letting something BE / not interfering (가만히 둬 = leave it alone). Note the meaning rides on the verb — 가만히 있다 is about your own body, 가만히 두다 is about not touching another thing. Don't confuse it with 조용히 (without noise): you can sit 가만히 yet keep talking. There's also a buried threat: 가만 안 둬 / 가만히 안 있을 거야 means 'I won't let this go,' so the same word can sound soothing or menacing purely by context. It frequently shortens to 가만 in speech (가만, 이게 뭐지? = 'wait, what's this?').

Missing the warning tone in 가만 안 둬 — beginners read it literally, but it's an idiom for 'you'll pay for this / I won't let it slide.'

usage: The most common pairing — documents, orders, contracts, bills
Reading every line and detail rather than skimming
Making sure absolutely nothing is left out
Weighing every detail before deciding or paying
examples: 천천히 꼼꼼히 봐.
Look it over slowly and carefully.
Bare advice; 꼼꼼히 pairs naturally with 천천히 — careful work isn't rushed
짐을 꼼꼼히 챙겼는데도 우산을 두고 왔어요.
Even though I packed carefully, I left my umbrella behind.
-는데도 = even though; shows 꼼꼼히 = leaving nothing out
사장님이 일을 꼼꼼히 가르쳐 주셨어요.
The boss taught me the work thoroughly.
A compliment — being called 꼼꼼하다 is high praise at a Korean workplace
nuance: 꼼꼼히 is the adverb of 꼼꼼하다 and describes doing something with careful, detail-by-detail attention, never skipping or rushing. In Korea being 꼼꼼하다 is a strong virtue — it's a top answer when describing your work strengths in an interview. The fine line with 자세히 is the key thing for learners: 자세히 is about the DEPTH of detail covered (자세히 설명하다 = explain in full detail), while 꼼꼼히 is about the CAREFULNESS of the doer (꼼꼼히 확인하다 = check meticulously so nothing is missed). It naturally attaches to 확인하다, 읽다, 챙기다, 따지다, and it ends in 히. The pitfall is pairing it with speed: 꼼꼼히 is inherently unhurried, so 꼼꼼히 빨리 jars — thoroughness and haste pull against each other.

usage: 충분히 잤어요 = I slept plenty / got enough sleep
Reassuring someone you completely get it
Confirming something is well within reach
examples: 시간 충분히 있어요.
There's plenty of time.
Bare reassurance to take the pressure off; 충분히 = enough and to spare
고기를 충분히 익혀서 드세요.
Cook the meat thoroughly before eating.
익히다 = cook through; here 충분히 = to a sufficient degree
그 마음 충분히 이해해요.
I completely understand how you feel.
Warm, empathetic; spoken 충분히 softens into 'completely/totally'
nuance: 충분히 comes from 充分 (充 'to fill' + 分 'portion/share', literally 'a full portion') and means a quantity or degree has been fully met — enough sleep, enough time, enough understanding. The key contrast for learners is with 완전히 (完全, 'complete'): 충분히 means 'enough for the purpose', not necessarily 100%, so 충분히 익히다 = cook it ENOUGH, while 완전히 익히다 = cook it ALL the way through. In conversation 충분히 also broadens into 'easily / readily' (충분히 그럴 수 있어요 = that could easily happen), which surprises learners expecting a literal amount. It's polite and supportive, which is why it floods comforting speech: 충분히 잘했어요, 충분히 이해해요.

Over-translating it as 'a lot' (많이); 충분히 means it MEETS the need, whereas 많이 just means a large amount with no judgment of sufficiency.

usage: Making your point unmistakable, leaving no room for doubt
분명히 기억나요 = I remember it for certain
Insisting something is so, often against pushback
분명히 올 거예요 = they'll definitely come
examples: 분명히 여기 뒀는데.
I definitely put it right here…
Bare, half to yourself, when something's gone missing — the classic 분명히 moment
다음부터는 분명히 말씀해 주세요.
Please tell me clearly from now on.
분명히 = unambiguously; a polite request for plain communication
분명히 어제까지 된다고 했잖아요.
You clearly said it'd be done by yesterday.
-잖아요 reminds the listener of a shared fact; 분명히 adds insistence
nuance: 분명히 comes from 分明 (分 'divide' + 明 'bright/clear', i.e. 'distinctly clear') and links two senses: stating something plainly ('clearly say'), and asserting strong certainty ('surely, definitely'). The second floods spoken Korean, especially the exasperated 분명히 …했는데 ('I definitely did X, but…') when reality contradicts you. The sharp contrast to learn is with 확실히 (確實): 분명히 leans on the SPEAKER'S own conviction and memory ('I'm sure I did'), while 확실히 points to OBJECTIVE, checkable fact ('it's confirmed'). So 분명히 그 사람이었어 = I'm certain it was him; 확실히 그 사람이었어 leans toward 'it's been verified'. Because 분명히 voices real confidence, it clashes with a hedge — pair guesses with 아마 (probably) instead.

Forgetting the plain 'clearly/distinctly' meaning — 분명히 말하다 is about clarity of statement, not just certainty.

usage: 확실히 알아보고 알려줄게요 = I'll check for certain and let you know
Pinning something down so there's no doubt later
examples: 약 먹으니까 확실히 낫네.
After the medicine I'm noticeably better.
Bare remark; here 확실히 = 'you can clearly tell' the difference
이건 확실히 해 둬야 나중에 문제가 없어요.
We should settle this clearly so there's no problem later.
확실히 해 두다 = nail it down / make sure
새 폰이 확실히 빠르긴 하네요.
The new phone is definitely faster, I'll give it that.
-긴 하다 concedes a point; 확실히 confirms an observed fact
nuance: 확실히 comes from 確實 (確 'firm/certain' + 實 'real/solid', i.e. 'firmly real') and means 'certainly, for sure' — but its most useful everyday flavor is 'noticeably', when you can plainly OBSERVE a difference: 확실히 빠르다 (clearly faster), 확실히 낫다 (clearly better). Set against 분명히, the divide is subjective vs objective: 분명히 voices the speaker's inner conviction, whereas 확실히 points to verifiable, demonstrable fact. The fixed phrase 확실히 하다 / 확실히 해 두다 ('make it definite / settle it for sure') is everywhere at work and in agreements. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping the 'noticeably' reading — learners hear 확실히 다르다 as 'surely different' when a Korean means 'you can clearly SEE it's different.'

usage: 간단히 먹읍시다 = let's just eat something light
Connector that sets up a concise summary
examples: 점심은 김밥으로 간단히 먹었어요.
I just had gimbap for a quick lunch.
간단히 + 먹다 is THE phrase for a light, fast meal
회의는 간단히 끝낼게요.
I'll keep the meeting short.
A polite promise at work to not drag things out
간단히 말하면 돈이 부족하다는 거예요.
Simply put, the point is there isn't enough money.
간단히 말하면 = in short / to sum up
nuance: 간단히 comes from 簡單 (簡 'brief/simple' + 單 'single', i.e. 'plain and single') and means doing something in a simple, brief, light way — a quick meal, a short explanation, a no-fuss finish. The crucial contrast is with 쉽게 (easily): 간단히 describes a small SCALE or effort, while 쉽게 describes low DIFFICULTY, so a task can be done 간단히 (quickly, lightly) yet still not be 쉽게 (it might be hard but short). The connector 간단히 말하면 ('in short') is a handy summarizing tool. The English-speaker trap is using it for a lavish meal or event — 간단히 inherently implies modest and light, so '간단히 잔치' (a simple feast) is a contradiction; for that you'd describe scale differently.

usage: Asking for or giving a full, detailed explanation
Examining something up close and carefully
Researching all the details before deciding
examples: 좀 더 자세히 말해 줘.
Tell me in a bit more detail.
Bare 반말 request; 자세히 = with more specifics, not louder or faster
계약 조건을 자세히 물어봤어요.
I asked about the contract terms in detail.
A smart move before signing anything in Korea
자세히 보니까 흠집이 있더라고요.
When I looked closely, there was a scratch.
-더라고요 reports a discovery; 자세히 보다 = inspect up close
nuance: 자세히 comes from 仔細 (仔 'careful' + 細 'fine/minute', i.e. 'down to the fine details') and means 'in detail / closely' — the natural opposite of 간단히. It pairs with 설명하다, 보다, 알아보다, 묻다 whenever you want full information rather than a quick gloss, and 자세히 설명해 주세요 is a survival phrase for getting specifics on contracts, services, and instructions in Korea. Two contrasts sharpen it: against 정확히 (正確, 'accurately'), 자세히 is about AMOUNT of detail while 정확히 is about CORRECTNESS — a long explanation can be 자세히 yet still wrong, hence not 정확히. And against 꼼꼼히, 자세히 describes the detail delivered, 꼼꼼히 the careful manner of the doer. It never describes a quantity of things, only thoroughness of explanation or observation.

It pairs with 설명하다, 보다, 알아보다, 묻다 whenever you want full information rather than a quick gloss, and 자세히 설명해 주세요 is a survival phrase for getting specifics on contracts, services, and instructions in Korea. It never describes a quantity of things, only thoroughness of explanation or observation.

Two contrasts sharpen it: against 정확히 (正確, 'accurately'), 자세히 is about AMOUNT of detail while 정확히 is about CORRECTNESS — a long explanation can be 자세히 yet still wrong, hence not 정확히. And against 꼼꼼히, 자세히 describes the detail delivered, 꼼꼼히 the careful manner of the doer.
자세히 comes from 仔細 (仔 'careful' + 細 'fine/minute', i.e. 'down to the fine details').

mistakes: Mixing up 자세히 (in detail) with 정확히 (accurately / exactly); detailed is not the same as precise — you can explain at length yet inaccurately.
Using 자세히 about an amount of items; it describes thoroughness of explaining or looking, not how much there is (use 많이 for quantity).
Confusing it with 꼼꼼히; 자세히 설명하다 (give lots of detail) is natural, while 꼼꼼히 fits checking/handling (꼼꼼히 확인하다).

usage: Letting something slip with no intent
A careless comment, often unexpectedly hurtful
examples: 무심코 한 말이었어요.
It was just something I said without thinking.
Bare apology/excuse; signals there was no bad intent
무심코 버튼을 눌렀다가 취소했어요.
I pressed the button without thinking, then canceled.
-았다가 = did it, then reversed; 무심코 = on autopilot
무심코 한 행동인데 오해를 샀어요.
It was a thoughtless act, but it caused a misunderstanding.
오해를 사다 = to invite a misunderstanding
nuance: 무심코 means doing or saying something absentmindedly, with no conscious intent, and it almost always sets up an UNINTENDED consequence — that's why it lives in apologies and reflections (무심코 한 말 = 'something I said without thinking'). It's built on 無心 (無 'without' + 心 'heart/mind', i.e. 'no mind/attention') plus the native suffix -코. The contrast to keep straight is the pair 무심코 vs 일부러 (on purpose): they're direct opposites, so 무심코 is your go-to when disclaiming intent. Don't confuse it with 무심하게, which means coldly/indifferently (a personality), whereas 무심코 means a one-off lapse of attention. The English-speaker pitfall is using it for anything planned — by definition 무심코 cannot describe a deliberate act.

Using 무심코 for a planned action; it specifically means there was no intention, so it clashes with anything deliberate.

english: on purpose; specially (going out of one's way)
usage: I didn't do it on purpose
The standard defense / apology after an accident
Going out of your way to see someone
Deliberately setting time aside for someone
Choosing not to do something on purpose
examples: 일부러 그런 거 아니에요.
I didn't do it on purpose.
Bare, high-frequency apology; the #1 use of 일부러
바쁠 텐데 일부러 와 줘서 고마워요.
Thanks for coming all this way even though you're busy.
The warm 'went out of your way' sense — a sincere thank-you
일부러 매운 걸 골랐어요, 스트레스 풀려고.
I picked something spicy on purpose, to relieve stress.
Shows clear 'deliberately' intent toward a goal
nuance: 일부러 (native Korean, no hanja) holds two everyday meanings English keeps apart: 'on purpose / intentionally', and 'going out of one's way / specially' to do a kindness. The first lives in apologies (일부러 그런 거 아니에요 = I didn't mean to), the second in thanks (일부러 와 줘서 고마워요 = thanks for making the special trip); both share the core of DELIBERATE effort, which makes it the opposite of 무심코. The contrast learners need is with 억지로 (reluctantly / by force): both involve doing something, but 일부러 is willing and intentional while 억지로 is against your will — 일부러 먹다 (eat on purpose, maybe for a reason) vs 억지로 먹다 (force yourself to eat). The pitfall is missing the warm 'special trip' reading and hearing only blame.

Missing the warm 'going out of your way' sense, which is very common in thank-yous (일부러 와 줘서 고마워요).
Over-using it for routine choices; for a plain decision Koreans often just state the action, reserving 일부러 for genuinely deliberate or out-of-the-way acts.

english: to one's heart's content, as much as you like
usage: eat as much as you like
Gracious host phrase at a meal
Telling someone to have a great time without holding back
to rest as much as you want
examples: 많이 차렸으니까 마음껏 드세요.
I made a lot, so please help yourself.
차리다 = set out food; warm 존댓말 hospitality
시험 끝났으니까 오늘은 마음껏 놀자.
The exam's over, so let's have all the fun we want today.
마음껏 놀다 = hang out / play with no restraint (반말)
휴가 동안 마음껏 쉬다 왔어요.
I rested as much as I wanted over the vacation.
A satisfied way to describe a good, unhurried break
nuance: 마음껏 means doing something fully and freely, to your heart's content, with no need to hold back — a generous, warm word that shines in hosting (마음껏 드세요) and in urging someone to enjoy or rest without restraint. It's 마음 ('heart/mind') + the native suffix -껏 ('to the very limit of'), the same -껏 you meet in 힘껏 (with all one's strength) and 정성껏 (with all one's care), so think of it as 'heart-to-the-max'. The contrast worth noting is with 실컷 (to one's fill / as much as one wants): the two overlap heavily, but 실컷 is more casual and often tied to satisfying an appetite or urge (실컷 자다 = sleep all you want), while 마음껏 sounds a touch warmer and more giving. The pitfall: it specifically means WITHOUT limits, so it clashes with any cap.
